method_note: FAST mode, one round. F-100 to F-115 reused with their sources from articles/2026-11-16-getting-married-in-france/02-research-B.json (which itself carries the NOIM facts from articles/2026-11-13-marriage-licence-requirements/02-research-A.json); not re-fetched today. F-116 to F-125 new, read today via Apify web-fetch from smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/vietnam, hcmc.consulate.gov.au (CNI page and legalisation page), hcmc.vietnam.embassy.gov.au (getting married overseas) and the HCCH Apostille status table. Vietnam Embassy in Australia pages surfaced only in a search summary and were not read, so they are not cited. A search summary quoting a CNI fee of AUD 177 from a wedding-planning site was not used. No competitor, aggregator or site/ draft used.

facts.claim: A Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, because local authorities may ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices across Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: At least one person applying for the CNI must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. Supporting documents: Australian citizen, a valid Australian passport; permanent resident, a valid foreign passport with evidence of permanent residence; foreign citizen partner, a valid foreign passport or photo ID; divorced, a Divorce Certificate; widowed, the deceased partner's Death Certificate. Originals or certified true copies; non-English documents need a professional English translation.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay on submission. DFAT advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Notarial services
facts.use_note: Write 'AUD 181 per CNI (2026 fee)' and 'AUD 105 per apostille (2026 fee)'. A search summary today quoted 'USD/AUD 102' for apostille or authentication from an older page; not used. Whether DFAT charges the same AUD 105 for an authentication (non-apostille) certificate was not confirmed (N-103).

facts.claim: DFAT does not publish a fixed processing time for legalisation: 'Processing times vary', with delays at peak holiday periods, when a request is incomplete or unpaid, or when DFAT must contact the document's issuing authority.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Getting married overseas

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA (recognition of foreign marriages).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Cite Part VA by name only; section text not read.

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: for a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent, must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: An Australian-born spouse married in Vietnam first registers a change of name with their state BDM; a Vietnamese certificate needs a full English translation.

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages: a person legally married in Australia can take their spouse's family name without registering a change of name (the exemption is worded for marriages in Australia). Foreign documents not in English must be translated in full and stamped by a NAATI-accredited translator, with copies of the original and the translation.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
facts.use_note: NSW only; other states not checked.

facts.claim: If you change your family name because of marriage, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one, and the Australian Passport Office recommends booking travel in the name that is in your passport.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office (DFAT)

facts.claim: Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip; some countries and some airlines apply a six-month validity rule, it can apply when transiting, and getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT)
facts.use_note: Write 'some countries', not 'many'. Vietnam-specific six-month rule only captured for visa extensions (F-125).

facts.claim: Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport; faster processing may be available for urgent travel at an extra fee.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT)

facts.claim: Legal at home, celebration abroad: Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.reused_from: marriage-licence-requirements A F-001 to F-005 (via getting-married-in-france B F-112)

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married

facts.claim: After an Australian ceremony the celebrant must submit the NOIM, the Declaration of No Legal Impediment and the Official Certificate of Marriage to the BDM registry in the state or territory where the marriage took place within 14 days.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Benefit of the home route: an Australian BDM certificate, which the Passport Office accepts directly (F-107).

facts.claim: A 'No Record of Marriage' certificate is requested from your state or territory BDM registry in Australia (the Australian Embassy France points couples to it where a certificate of single status is required).
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: France context only. For Vietnam, the Australian Consulate-General HCMC says Australians do NOT need to give Vietnamese authorities a single status certificate (F-121). Do not tell Vietnam couples to order one unless the Wedded Advisor confirms a local office asks.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's Vietnam page says you need a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) if you plan to marry in Vietnam. Apply for it through the Australian Embassy in Hanoi or the Australian Consulate-General in Ho Chi Minh City, or from DFAT in Australia. Fees apply.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Vietnam travel advice
facts.use_note: CNI answer: yes, the Australian missions in Vietnam (Hanoi embassy and HCMC consulate-general) issue a CNI. Page 'still current at 17 November 2026', last updated 24 September 2026.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's Vietnam page says that a CNI obtained from DFAT in Australia must be authenticated by the embassy or consulate of Vietnam in Australia, and only then will the Department of Justice in Vietnam recognise it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Vietnam travel advice
facts.use_note: CONFLICT with F-118. Smartraveller still describes the consular legalisation route (DFAT document, then authentication by Vietnam's embassy or consulate in Australia). The HCCH depositary shows the Apostille Convention in force for Viet Nam since 11 September 2026, with Australia a party, which would normally replace Vietnamese consular legalisation with a DFAT apostille. Smartraveller's marriage wording may predate the change. Writer should say: get the CNI in Vietnam from the Australian mission where possible (F-119, no Australian legalisation step needed), or, if getting it from DFAT in Australia, confirm with DFAT and the Embassy of Vietnam in Canberra whether an apostille alone is now accepted. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process. Vietnamese embassy legalisation fees not found (N-102).

facts.claim: HCCH status table for the 1961 Apostille Convention (last update 30 June 2026): Viet Nam acceded on 31 December 2025 with entry into force on 11 September 2026 (marked A**, meaning one or more contracting states objected to the accession); Australia has been a party since 16 March 1995.
facts.publisher: Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH), Apostille Convention status table
facts.use_note: Treaty depositary, official. Conflicts with F-117 on the practical route, hence low. Which states objected is not shown on this table; a search summary (law-firm sources, not cited) named Austria, Czechia and Germany, not Australia. No DFAT page read today confirms DFAT now apostilles documents for Vietnam (N-101).

facts.claim: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City: Australian citizens, citizens of another country domiciled in Australia, and Australian permanent residents who intend to marry in Vietnam must submit a CNI when registering the marriage with Vietnamese authorities; the Vietnamese government has the authority to solemnise marriages in Vietnam. To apply: book a 'Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage' appointment under Notarial Services, complete the application form but do not sign it (a Consular Officer must witness the signature), and attend with originals or certified true copies of: your Australian passport (or foreign passport with Australian permanent resident visa) and divorce or death certificate if applicable; your partner's passport or ID card (for example a Vietnamese passport or ID) and divorce or death certificate if applicable. The fee is non-refundable and payable in Vietnamese dong by bank card only. The CNI, in English and Vietnamese, is available for collection the following working day, 9:00am to 12:00pm.
facts.publisher: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City, Applying for a CNI
facts.use_note: Page undated. Means at least one trip to the consulate in person before the wedding, with a next-day turnaround. Hanoi embassy procedure not read separately (N-100). VND fee amount not captured (N-102). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City: documents provided in a language other than English must be accompanied by an official English translation, done by Notary Offices or professional translation services in Vietnam.
facts.publisher: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City, Applying for a CNI
facts.use_note: This covers documents given to the consulate (for example a Vietnamese partner's papers into English). Rules for translating Australian documents into Vietnamese for Vietnamese authorities were NOT found on an official page (N-104).

facts.claim: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City: Australian citizens are not required to submit a Statutory Declaration of their marital status, a Single Status Certificate or a Divorce Certificate to Vietnamese local authorities.
facts.publisher: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City, Applying for a CNI
facts.use_note: The CNI does that job for Vietnamese authorities. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process with the local office.

facts.claim: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City legalisation page: legalisation verifies the signature, seal or stamp on an Australian public document, after which the mission attaches an apostille or an authentication certificate. Applicants should ask the receiving authority which documents they need legalised and whether they need an apostille or an authentication, and confirm the documents are eligible for DFAT legalisation. Damaged, framed or laminated documents are not accepted.
facts.publisher: Australian Consulate-General Ho Chi Minh City, Legalisation / Authentication / Apostille
facts.use_note: Page does not say which of the two Vietnamese authorities now want; it defers to the receiving authority. Supports the 'ask first' wording in F-117.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's overall advice level for Vietnam is 'Exercise normal safety precautions' (still current at 17 November 2026; updated 24 September 2026). The latest update notes Vietnam's storm season is usually from June to November, with heavy rain, floods, landslides and typhoons that may affect flights, roads and power.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Vietnam travel advice
facts.use_note: Storm season is relevant to wedding date choice; batch A climate facts should align. Levels can change at short notice; link the page.

facts.claim: To enter Vietnam you must have a visa or a visa exemption certificate; Australian passport holders can't get a visa on arrival. Vietnam offers an eVisa for tourism or business that, if granted, may allow a stay of up to 90 days with single or multiple entries. Apply only through the official eVisa website (evisa.gov.vn), check your details when lodging and again on receipt, and consider printing a hard copy because of reported difficulties accessing eVisas at airport check-in. Entry and exit conditions can change at short notice.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Vietnam travel advice
facts.use_note: Applies to the couple and every Australian guest. eVisa fee not captured (N-105).

facts.claim: Smartraveller Vietnam: if your spouse or parent is a Vietnamese national, you can apply for a visa exemption certificate. You can't change the status of your entry visa to another visa type in Vietnam, and to get a visa extension from Vietnamese immigration your passport must have at least 6 months validity left at the time of application.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Vietnam travel advice
facts.use_note: Visa exemption certificate is for couples where one partner is Vietnamese; mention only in that context.

legal.summary: A CNI is needed to marry in Vietnam; issued by the Australian Embassy Hanoi, the Consulate-General HCMC, or DFAT in Australia. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

Smartraveller: a DFAT-issued CNI must be authenticated by Vietnam's embassy or consulate in Australia before Vietnam's Department of Justice recognises it. Conflicts with Apostille Convention entry into force for Vietnam (F-118). Confirm with DFAT and the Embassy of Vietnam in Canberra; Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Apostille Convention in force for Viet Nam from 11 September 2026 (HCCH depositary). Practical acceptance of Australian apostilles not yet confirmed by DFAT or Vietnam's embassy.

Marriage solemnised and registered by Vietnamese authorities; Australians submit a CNI, obtainable in person at the HCMC consulate (English and Vietnamese, next working day). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
No single status certificate or statutory declaration needed by Vietnamese local authorities for Australian citizens. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in Vietnam and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Passport in married name: Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Legal at home route: NOIM to an authorised celebrant 1 to 18 months ahead; celebrant physically present. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
